extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, students of drama, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging Tragedy (plot, character, diction, chorus, and staging), drawn from Aristotle's Poetics with commentary and examples. Emphasizes plot construction (tying/loosing), character delineation, believable disclosure, brevity, and rhetorical diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking of projection/perpetration scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: There are only real alternatives: either they perpetrate an atrocity or not, and consciously or not (doing or not, and with knowledge or not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic ranking: conscious projection without perpetration is the worst (shocking without catharsis), conscious projection with perpetration is next worst, unconscious projection with perpetration followed by disclosure is better (shocking element absent, disclosure thrilling), and the best is unconscious projection without perpetration (e.g. Cresphontes, Iphigeneia, Helle). Use these forms deliberately to control shock, pity, and terror.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be good
rubrics_metrics.description: The first and most important aim in delineation of character is that the characters should be good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We require persons with whom we can sympathize; without them the dramatist cannot arouse or gratify interest. Aristotle argues there should be no villain in the piece (villainy tends toward the comic). Only introduce badness when it is justified by part, class, or contrast (e.g., Aegisthus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character appropriateness (species-suitable traits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character traits must be appropriate: the species of a virtue must suit the person (e.g., a woman's form of courage may differ and be suitable to her role).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making a person possess types of virtue or behavior that are unsuitable for their social/biological role on stage (theatrical appropriateness). Consider audience expectations and social roles when assigning traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be like (fidelity to historical character)
rubrics_metrics.description: The historical character portrayed must not be seriously altered in reproduction; e.g., Achilles must not be made cowardly, Odysseus brainless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some departure is allowed to produce aesthetic effect, but avoid puzzling the spectator by altering a leading trait of a famous character. Degree of permissible alteration depends on public and celebrity of the character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equability (consistency of character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the character portrayed is fitful, the portrayal ought to be uniformly fitful (consistent within the chosen type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not produce sudden, unjustified shifts in character (e.g., Iphigeneia in Aulis being unlike her later self). Consistency may be of a negative trait (fitful) but must be maintained throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech and conduct must reveal intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Speech or conduct is psychological if it reveals any intention with which a course is adopted or rejected, and the character delineated will be good if the intention be so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialogue and actions to show motives and intentions; characterization is judged by the moral quality of those intents as revealed in speech/conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should evolve from characters (no deus ex machina)
rubrics_metrics.description: The evolution of the story should come about from the characters themselves, and not by a deus ex machina; the deus ex machina may be employed only for events in the background (primeval mysteries or futurity requiring revelation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid introducing external, unmotivated agents to resolve central action. If supernatural revelation is necessary, confine it to background explanation or to things the audience can accept as divine knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: No unaccountable occurrences in the foreground
rubrics_metrics.description: In the proceedings themselves there should be nothing unaccountable; if there is, it should be in the background of the play, as in the Oedipus of Sophocles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreground events must be intelligible, probable, and causally motivated within the world of the play; inexplicable miracles or absurd reversals onstage harm the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow laws of nature and moral certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: In character and incident you should always study laws of nature and moral certainty so that what occurs becomes either necessary or morally certain for the kind of character to say or do the thing, and in the particular order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for psychological and moral plausibility: actions should feel necessary or inevitable given characters' natures and the moral logic of the situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of mistaken identity — prefer naturally probable revelations
rubrics_metrics.description: The best Disclosure of Mistaken Identity proceeds without violation of probability from the actual composition of the story (e.g., Oedipus, Iphigeneia); other methods are ranked below.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred methods (from best to worse): natural/unforced revelation within the plot; observation of coincidence; mention/sight that agitates the hero; tokens (congenital or acquired) are least scientific. Avoid fabricated proofs inserted by the poet that the story itself doesn't warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tokens vs. scientific proofs — prefer general (scientific) signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Tokens (spears, scars, necklaces) are unscientific signs tied to individuals; 'scientific' signs are those that belong to whole classes of cases and are therefore preferable for disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor revelations that would naturally occur or be probable for any person in similar circumstances; rely less on singular tokens unless they serve a stronger dramatic purpose (or reveal identity contrary to intention, which is superior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading the audience via disappointed expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: When you introduce a surprise it should be in the form of a disappointed expectation: the spectator had made up his mind that something definite would happen, and suddenly it all changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use misdirection that plays on audience expectations fairly; do not reveal the plot in a way that betrays internal probability or construction (avoid cheap tricks that violate the story's logic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualize the story — compose as living pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: While composing the story and helping it out with diction, visualize it; the poet will thus be, as it were, an eyewitness of the events, most likely to discover what is appropriate and alive to inconsistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think the drama in pantomime/visual terms; stage the action in images rather than relying solely on linguistic description. This helps catch inconsistencies and ensures scenic viability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gesture and genuine feeling to inform performance
rubrics_metrics.description: While composing, assist the work by your gestures so far as possible; a fictitious emotion emanating from a reality of the same kind is most realistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and actors should use embodied rehearsal—gestures and remembered feeling—to produce realistic portrayal. There is debate among theorists, but embodiment aids realism when well controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare argument/abstract before scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the argument has already been treated or whether you are treating it for the first time, the argument should be first stated in the abstract, then filled in with scenes to the requisite length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the principles and central argument you wish to illustrate (the 'logic' of the play) before composing scenes and dialogue. Scenes and names should then be germane to that argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenes must be concise in tragedy (avoid romance-length interludes)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a play the scenes are concise; in a Romance they are spun out. A Tragedy must not be turned into a Romance — avoid endless interludes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain dramatic economy: trim episodic or irrelevant digressions that dilute the tragic arc. Treat long sagas as series of plays or select a compact portion appropriate to tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tying and loosing — structural division of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: In every Tragedy one part is the tying, the other the loosing. A real tying stretches from the commencement to the exact point at which the change of fortune commences; a real loosing occupies from transition-point to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize plot so that the 'tying' (setup, antecedent history) leads inevitably to a clear transition, after which the 'loosing' (unraveling, catastrophe/resolution) follows. Master both sections for successful tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to combine four varieties of Tragedy where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four varieties: Plot Tragedy (irony of fate/mistaken identity), Emotional Tragedy (pathos), Psychological Tragedy, and Tragedy of appropriate expression; try to combine the beauties of all four if you can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If synthesis is impossible, include as many effective elements as possible; modern audiences may unfairly expect mastery of all types, but focus on the strongest suitable elements for your story and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity of Tragedies defined by story (tying/loosing), not mere characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing should decide the identity of Tragedies equally with the Story; the identity of Stories is decided by the matter which can be identically tied and loosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different plays can share characters but be distinct if their tying/loosing (story arcs) differ; conversely, identical loosing would make stories the same despite different names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus as participant/actor — integral to action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus should regard itself as one of the actors and a member of the entirety, and should participate in the performance (Sophocles style) rather than be detachable songs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make choric songs and action integral to the plot and emotional development; avoid re-using or transferring choric material between plays. The chorus can initiate emotion and steer audience sympathy (psychology of crowds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction/Intelligence: speech as instrument for demonstration, refutation, and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: To the province of Intelligence belong all operations of which Speech is the instrument: demonstration and refutation, the arousing of emotions (pity, fear, anger), exaggeration and depreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft speech to perform rhetorical functions appropriate to scene and effect. Use modes of stating (style) to render matter agreeable and to produce intended emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of sentences (elocutionary forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of Sentences: knowledge of Command, Prayer, Narrative, Menace, Question, Reply, etc. belongs to elocution and informs how speech is used in drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply sentence types and speech acts deliberately according to their function in the scene; while poets need not be experts, awareness of these forms improves dramatic efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study Prosody and phonetic building blocks of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of Speech include Letter, Combination, Conjunction, Noun, Verb, Inflexion, Statement. Letters (vowel, semi-vowel, mute) differ in mouth shape, breathing, length, intonation; these differences should be studied in Prosody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to phonetics, rhythm, and prosodic features to make verse and spoken language suitable for performance and to control auditory effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect audience prejudices and impressions indirectly related to art
rubrics_metrics.description: While observing rules the poet should be careful of the impressions only indirectly connected with his art; a tragedy must have psychology but need not trench on religion or politics, and if it does the prejudices of the audience should not be hurt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt content to the audience's religious, political, and cultural sensibilities when possible or be prepared for adverse reception; some effective plays fail for later generations because underlying assumptions change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select stories/families that naturally afford catastrophic situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Playwrights, seeking to furnish such situations in their plots, discovered that certain plots somehow contained them, and have been compelled to resort to the families in which such catastrophes came about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose source material (families, myths, stories) that naturally produce the tragic situations you wish to stage, rather than forcing catastrophes where they don't belong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary knavery or immoral psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: An example of immoral psychology is any unnecessary case of knavery; a poet can only be charged with immorality when he introduces a knave without anything making such introduction necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce villainous or deceitful behavior only when justified by class, contrast, or necessity within the plot; arbitrary immorality undermines artistic and moral credibility.
